--- A version of Weierstrass' Theorem for unbounded monotone sequences ---

Hello.
Weierstrass theorem is a theorem about convergence of, uh, of bounded and monotone sequences.
And to complete this theory, uh, I would like to show you the the following, which is a slightly
theoretical video.
And it will show you a kind of generalization of wire stress theorem, uh, to unbounded sequences.
Let's start a version of virus theorem for unbounded monotone sequences.
And this is this theorem in two versions.
The first one is a theorem, and the second one is just.
Corollary.
If xn is increasing or at least non-decreasing and not bounded above.
Then a limit with n tending to infinity of x n is plus infinity, and immediate consequence of this
theorem is the following.
A kind of mirroring.
If a y n is decreasing or non-increasing and not bounded below, then its limit must be minus infinity.
And well, the Weierstrass theorem that you have seen until now was formulated in video 108, in calculus
one, part one.
And then you got this proof, and I show you this slide.
Now to refer to video 24 of the current course, when where I walked you through this proof one more
time.
And why do I do this.
Well because maybe after having seen this present video, you would like to go back to video 24 and
listen one more time for this explanation, and then you will see a striking similarity between this
proof and the proof that I'm going to show you in this lecture.
So just remember this that.
Well here we found some an epsilon for which a and epsilon was to the right of c minus epsilon.
And then because of monotonicity, the entire remaining part of this sequence is also to the right of
c minus epsilon which kind of completed our proof.
And now you will see something very similar.
But before I start proving, I would like to to make such a remark that the meaning of this theorem,
in combination with our regular good old Weierstrass theorem, is the following.
Monotone on sequences bounded or not always converge in the extended R, and you remember that the extended
R is the entire R with two additional objects A plus infinity and minus infinity.
So if a sequence is bounded and and monotone, then it is convergent to a number, but it is if it is
unbounded and monotone depending, or if it's not unbounded and monotone depending on if it's increasing
or decreasing, it will converge in extended R either to plus or to minus infinity.
So this is the nice thing with this new theorem that together with this old one, tells us that monotone
sequences always behave in a convergent way in the extended r.
So first, before I start proving the theorem, I would like to explain why this corollary really follows
immediately.
Well, and I, I used the word mirroring that it's kind of mirrored situation.
And you will see in the next slide that it's really about mirroring because by definition a limit with
n tending to infinity of y n is equal to minus infinity if and only if limit with n tending to infinity
of opposite to y is plus infinity.
And this is this mirroring illustration that you got in calculus one, part one in video 114.
Here we have a example of a sequence that tends to plus infinity and minus infinity.
So this is here our original sequence that tends to minus infinity.
And here you got the information that by definition it means that the sequence of the opposite elements
tends to plus infinity.
So you see that if we are.

Ratio test for sequences.

It says that if an is such a sequence of non-zero numbers that the sequence of absolute values of the
ratios of its consecutive terms is convergent, and its limit is equal to a g that is some real number.
Then, if this limit g is less than one and obviously it must be a positive or zero because, um, because
the elements of this new sequence are zero or more, so it cannot be negative.
Then an is convergent and an tends to zero.
If g is greater than one, then an is divergent, and the sequence of absolute values of an tends to
plus infinity.
And in this particular case, we can also consider g equal to plus infinity.
And if g is equal to one, then the test is inconclusive and is.
You need to look for a different method.

the sequence an and or.
Well, generally, if you don't need to imagine, and if you don't want to imagine any positivity,

even decrease to zero, right?
And actually often very often If you have this one and you can determine the limit, you can simply

n tending to infinity.

--- Absolute and conditional convergence ---

Hello.
This lecture is the last one in this section that contains really essential information.
After that, you get a five videos with just some playful stuff with interesting series that are not
really very, very famous, but but really fun to work with.
But this one is really important, so pay attention.
Absolute and conditional convergence.
So this is the plan for this lecture.
I will not read everything to you right now.
I will just, uh, start with a some problem formulation.
So with each series of this type we can associate another series that has as elements the absolute values
of the elements of our original series.
And we can discuss the convergence of this series and the convergence of the associated series with
absolute values.
And if a series has only positive or at least non-negative elements, then its sequence of partial sums
is increasing or at least non-decreasing.
You have seen it before.
I have used this argument when I told you about power series and we well, it was mentioned many times,
and you remember that each a monotone sequence is either convergent to some number if it is bounded
or divergent to plus infinity.
If it is not bounded above, there is no third possibility.
Right.
So this means that the series.
This series with absolute values can only be convergent if the sequence of partial sums is bounded or
divergent to plus infinity.
If the sequence of partial sums is unbounded, and, it follows from these two theorems that are called
Weierstrass theorems, and.
This is why I will often write like this for series series with non-negative elements.
This simply means that the series is convergent because they are only two possibilities either convergence
to a number or divergence to plus infinity.
And as there is no other options, then this can only be interpreted as that the series is convergent
to a number.
So for series with non-negative elements, this simply means that the series is convergent, and this
is a common way of writing it down.
So now we will work with this to these two types of series.
This one can be obviously convergent or divergent, and this can be convergent to a non-negative number
or divergent to plus infinity.
But it cannot be just divergent.
And the series.
Our original series is called absolutely convergent.
If the corresponding series with elements with absolute values is convergent.
So this is the definition of absolutely convergent series.
Such a series is absolutely convergent if the corresponding series with absolute values is convergent,
and if the corresponding series diverges to plus infinity.
But our original series is convergent, then obviously not absolutely convergent, right?
Then it is called conditionally convergent.
So these two terms are excluding each other, right.
A series can either be absolutely convergent or conditionally convergent or divergent of course.
So these two mean that our series is convergent.
But it is absolutely convergent.
If also the corresponding series with absolute values is convergent, otherwise it is just conditionally
convergent.
So first remark or a theorem.
If a series is absolutely convergent, then it is also convergent.
How to prove this?
Well, we will use for this the Cauchy condition for a series, which tells us that a series is convergent
if and only if this holds.
So for each epsilon, there exists such an epsilon that for all n that are greater than or equal to
this n epsilon, and for all k that are positive natural numbers, such a absolute value of such a sum
is less than epsilon.
So this is a piece of a of a partial sum a indexed by n plus k without the, uh, the head.
And the head is the piece of partial sum, uh, with indexes of a starting with one and ending by n.
So this is an if and only if condition for convergence.
So now we have by triangle inequality we know that this inequality holds right.
So if our um series is absolutely convergent, it means that the series with absolute values around
the elements satisfies this condition.
And by um transitivity of inequality, then the original series also satisfies the same condition and
we are done.
So this is really not difficult.
That absolute convergence implies convergence.
But the converse is not true.
So it is not true that if a series is convergent, then it must be absolutely convergent.
What is an example?
The simplest example we can take is the harmonic series, which is clearly divergent to plus infinity.
Uh, but uh, the um, the the alternating harmonic series is convergent.
So this series is convergent but is not absolutely convergent.
Because you see, for this series, the series series with absolute values would be simply this one
which is divergent.
So this, This series is convergent but just conditionally convergent.
And this was motivated in videos with these numbers you can have a look if you want to.
But I believe that by now we know these two guys very well.
So in other words this series is just conditionally convergent.
But for geometric series this theorem is if and only if because.
Well, for a geometric series it's a series with absolute values.
Looks like this.
This is just a number.
So it doesn't matter a constant number which you can factor out if you want to.
It doesn't it doesn't influence convergence or divergence in any way.
And you know that these two series are both convergence convergent.
If the quotient Q to absolute value is less than one.
So um.
In other words, all convergent geometric series are also absolutely convergent.
